Working notes · Susenas September 2025

MBG and poverty: what we did, what we found, and what we still don't know

A complete walkthrough of the Susenas September 2025 analysis — the measurement problem, how the transfer was identified and valued, every check that was run, and all the results in one place.

01 The problem in one page

In one line: MBG meals are already counted inside the official poverty statistics, but nothing in the data says which rupiah came from the programme — so we had to recover it.

Susenas enumerators record food a household ate but did not buy, valued at local prices. That includes MBG trays. So the transfer flows into FOOD, then EXPEND, then KAPITA — the per-capita expenditure that BPS uses to compute poverty. The published 8.25% headcount for September 2025 already includes MBG.

That creates the question this whole exercise answers: what would poverty have been without it? To answer, we must subtract the transfer. To subtract it, we must first know its value. And the value is not recorded anywhere — column B41K8 lumps MBG together with kenduri food, gifts from relatives, workplace meals and own production.

The core difficulty

We know exactly who received MBG (question M1106) and how often (M1108). We do not know what it was worth. Everything in sections 3–6 is about closing that gap without accidentally counting ordinary gifts as programme benefits.

02 What the survey actually gives us

In one line: 13.6 juta recipients in 10.4 juta households, averaging 5.82 meals per household per week — and the KP and Modul files link household-to-household via URUT.
13.6 juta
people received MBG in the survey week
10.4 juta
households with at least one recipient (14.0%)
5.82
meals per recipient household per week
21.5%
of school children received it

The MBG questions sit in Blok XI of the Modul questionnaire, at the individual level. The consumption data sits in a separate file. They join on the household id URUT, which we verified links 1:1 across all five files.

School children are 94% of all recipients. The other target arms — balita, ibu hamil, ibu menyusui — had barely started (2–4% coverage). So in practice this is a school feeding programme, measured in its scale-up phase.

03 Why the obvious method fails

In one line: comparing recipients to non-recipients gives Rp 43,930 per week, but the same comparison says recipients also get Rp 793 more free cigarettes — which no tray contains.

The natural approach is to compare the free-food value of recipient and non-recipient households and call the difference the programme. On prepared rice meals that gives 59,246 − 15,316 = Rp 43,930 per household per week.

It is wrong, because MBG targets households with school children. Those households differ from others in many ways that also affect how much free food they receive. The comparison therefore mixes the programme with everything else that makes those households different.

The proof it's contaminated. In-kind value by recipient status, Rp per household per week.
ItemRecipientsNon-recipientsGapWhat it means
Nasi campur/rames59,24615,31643,930Plausibly the meal
Susu cair pabrik3,729913,638Plausibly the milk
Rokok kretek filter2,2621,469793Cigarettes are not on any MBG tray

That last row is the whole argument. If this method says recipients "receive" Rp 793 more free cigarettes, then it is measuring something other than the programme — and we cannot tell how much of the Rp 43,930 is that same something. Two other signs point the same way: non-recipients already receive Rp 15,316 of free prepared rice (free food is normal in Indonesian social life), and recipient households eat more fruit in total simply because they contain children.

04 The dose-response idea

In one line: stop comparing recipients to non-recipients; instead compare recipients who got more meals with recipients who got fewer.

If a rupiah of free food really comes from MBG, it must scale with the number of meals delivered. Ordinary gifts have no reason to. So we throw away the recipient / non-recipient comparison entirely and use only variation in intensity among households that all receive the programme.

recdaysi = sum over members of ( days received ) A household with two children fed four days each has recdays = 8. Range 1–40, mean 5.82.
value of item ki = αk + βk × recdaysi + γk × household sizei + error Estimated on recipient households only, weighted, robust standard errors. β is the rupiah of item k that arrives with one extra meal.

Three things make this work, and they are worth remembering:

  • Recipients only. Everyone in the sample is treated, so the selection that ruins the naive comparison cannot operate.
  • The intercept is a bin. Whatever ordinary gift-giving these households enjoy goes into α, not β. That is exactly the contamination the naive method could not remove.
  • Household size is controlled, because bigger households have more eligible children and consume more of everything.

05 Proving it works: the placebo battery

In one line: the ~200 items that are not MBG behave exactly like random noise (KS test p = 0.583), and the nine carriers sit far out in the tail.

A single placebo would not be enough. The strongest test uses all of them at once: we run the same regression on every food item. Nine turn out to be carriers; the other 143 are placebos by construction. If the design is clean, their t-statistics should look like draws from a standard normal.

How to read that chart

It is worth going slowly here, because this one figure carries most of the weight of the whole method.

What was computed. For every single food item in the consumption module — all 152 of them, from rice to cigarettes to salak — we ran the same regression: does the free (unpurchased) value of this item rise with the number of MBG meals the household received? Each of those 152 regressions produces one t-statistic: how many standard errors the relationship sits away from zero. That single number per item is what the horizontal axis shows.

The logic. If an item has nothing to do with MBG, its true relationship with meals is zero, so its t-statistic is pure noise. Statistical theory says such noise follows a standard normal distribution: centred on 0, standard deviation 1, about 95% of values between −1.96 and +1.96. So we take the 143 items we did not classify as MBG and ask whether they look like noise.

What each element on the chart is.
ElementWhat it represents
Blue barsThe 143 non-MBG items, binned by their t-statistic
Grey curveWhat pure noise should look like — a standard normal, N(0,1)
Dashed lines±1.96, the 5% significance threshold
Orange trianglesThe nine MBG carrier items, at their t-values

What it shows. The blue histogram sits almost exactly on the grey curve: mean −0.055 where 0 is expected, standard deviation 1.084 where 1 is expected, 6.29% falling outside the dashed lines where 5% is expected, and a formal test nowhere near rejecting (p = 0.583).

That is what rules out the thing we were worried about. If recdays were secretly a proxy for something else — wealth, sociability, a general "these households receive more of everything" effect — then many items would show spurious relationships and the blue distribution would be too wide or shifted off-centre. It is neither.

And the nine orange triangles sit at t = 3.0 to 19.3, completely outside where noise lives. That is the second half of the argument: the items we call MBG are not marginally significant items that might be flukes — they are so far beyond the noise range that chance cannot produce them.

Two things that trip people up

Some blue bars do cross the dashed lines, and that is correct. Five percent of pure noise is supposed to exceed ±1.96 — that is what a 5% threshold means. Seeing 6.29% out there confirms the theory rather than contradicting it. It is also exactly why the carrier selection needs false-discovery-rate control rather than a raw 5% cut.

The triangles' height means nothing. They sit on an arbitrary rug below the axis; only their left-right position — their t-value — carries information. And the rightmost one, nasi campur at t = 19.3, is plotted beyond the labelled part of the axis, so it looks like it is floating at the edge. It is simply very far to the right.

The rest of the battery. Each family is chosen so the programme cannot affect it.
TestWhat it checkstVerdict
A1 tobacco, in-kindDo gift networks track meal count?−1.13flat — pass
A3 bumbu, in-kindSame, different goods−0.52flat — pass
A4 non-tray fruitsAre only tray fruits affected?1.09flat — pass
A2 kopi / teh, in-kindAssumed adult-only−2.77FAILS — see below
C housing, permit, electricity, educationThings a week of meals cannot change|t| < 1.8all flat — pass
Child / elderly shareMechanically tied to eligibility15.2 / −7.7not a placebo
The strongest single number

Home ownership, building permits, electricity and the head's education together explain 0.2% of the variation in meals received. A week of school meals cannot change any of them, so if the dose were really a proxy for wealth, they would predict it. They do not.

One test failed, and we kept it in

A2 (coffee and tea) slopes with dose, t = −2.77. We had flagged this risk in advance: children drink sweet tea, so coffee and tea are not adult-only goods in an Indonesian household. A2 is therefore not a valid placebo. It is reported, but it does not count as evidence for the design.

06 What a meal is worth

In one line: Rp 7,491 per meal, spread across nine food items — and the answer barely moves however you select them.
The nine carrier items. Rupiah per additional meal, from the dose regression.
CodeItemRp/mealtMenu part
196Nasi campur/rames6,30919.3the tray itself
79Susu cair pabrik53210.8milk
207Ayam/daging matang2423.6protein
130Jeruk1455.2fruit
140Semangka1177.0fruit
150Melon424.7fruit
215Sari buah kemasan413.4drink
152Kelengkeng413.2fruit
136Salak213.0fruit
Total per meal7,491—sum of the nine

The fruits that show up are exactly the sliceable tray fruits; the other fourteen fruit items are flat. That internal consistency is reassuring — the method is picking out a real menu, not random items.

Rp 7,491 sits below the programme's ~Rp 10,000 per-portion budget — consistent, but this is not a validation. Several wedges separate the two numbers and they do not all point the same way. Overheads (packaging, transport, kitchen labour) and plate waste push the household-side value below the cost. But measurement pushes our estimate below the true value: recall error in the days variable attenuates the coefficient, and the respondent may not fully record food a child ate at school. Meanwhile retail markup over the programme's bulk procurement pushes the other way. The mapping from cost to household value is therefore ambiguous, and if the true consumed value were Rp 10,000, attenuation alone could still deliver an estimate of 7,491.

Consequence worth remembering

Rp 7,491 is best read as a lower bound on the value households consumed. That means the poverty impact below (0.326 pp) is understated on the valuation margin even while being an upper bound on the behavioural margin (ρ = 0) — the two biases run in opposite directions. S3, which values meals at the full Rp 10,000, partially brackets the valuation side from above. The estimate's credibility rests on the placebo battery and the specification robustness, not on the comparison with the programme budget.

Does the selection rule matter? Barely.
RuleCarriersRp per meal
Raw 5% significance107,504
5% with false-discovery-rate control (what we use)97,491
Conservative |t| > 397,491

The only disputed item is susu kental manis (condensed milk), worth Rp 13 per meal. Nothing rides on it.

Regional variation — real, but not about prices

Per-meal value differs across the six regions (Sumatera 5,893 · Jawa 7,487 · Bali-Nusra 9,535 · Kalimantan 9,733 · Sulawesi 6,786 · Maluku-Papua 9,982; joint test p = 0.0085). But it does not track food prices — Sumatera has high food prices and the lowest value; Bali-Nusra has low prices and nearly the highest. So this reflects what is on the tray and how established local kitchens were, not the cost of the same basket. Never describe it as a price adjustment.

07 The crowd-out story (we were wrong once)

In one line: a first attempt suggested the design was broken; it turned out the specification was missing household composition, and once fixed, total spending rises by exactly the transfer — but too imprecisely to prove it.

If a household gets free meals, does it spend less of its own money on food? That is the crowd-out rate ρ. It matters because the counterfactual is KAPITA_cf = (EXPEND − (1−ρ) × v) / size: at ρ = 0 the transfer adds fully to consumption, at ρ = 1 it displaces own spending and changes nothing.

Our first attempt looked alarming. Regressing total expenditure on meals gave a coefficient 2.5 times the transfer's own value — impossible as a causal effect, implying a nonsense crowd-out of −146%. It looked like the design had failed.

What was actually going on. Coefficients per additional weekly meal, Rp per month.
ControlsTransferTotal spendingt
Household size only7,49179,1133.04
+ child share7,47294,6853.60
+ school-age share7,41042,5821.51
+ province and urban/rural7,38431,8781.14
Transfer value for comparison: Rp 31,645/month. The valuation moves 1.4% across all four rows.
The resolution

The confounder was household composition, not income. Households getting more meals contain more school-age children, because that is who is eligible. Once school-age share and geography are controlled, total spending rises by Rp 31,878 against a transfer worth Rp 31,645 — implying ρ ≈ 0. Consumption rises by the full value of the meals. And crucially, the valuation itself barely moved, which is the robustness we needed.

But we still cannot report ρ

That coefficient's 95% interval runs from −22,840 to 86,597, which maps to ρ anywhere from −1.74 to 1.72. The point estimate sits at zero, the anomaly is gone, but the data cannot exclude anything. So ρ stays a reported assumption, not a finding — every result below is shown across ρ = 0 to 0.5, with 0 as the benchmark.

One more piece of support: every single recipient household buys more food than the transfer is worth (mean transfer Rp 187k/month against Rp 2.93 juta of purchased food). When a transfer is small relative to what you already buy, it behaves like cash — the standard argument for ρ near zero.

08 Who actually gets MBG

In one line: coverage is urban-skewed and roughly flat across income — the rural poor half is 26% of the eligible population but receives 16% of the meals.

This is an early-rollout pattern: kitchens were established first where they were easiest to run. It matters for the poverty results below, because a transfer that misses the poorest reduces poverty less than the same money would if better targeted.

09 The poverty results

In one line: MBG kept about 923,000 people out of poverty in that week — the headcount would have been 8.58% instead of 8.25%.
Validation first

Computing poverty on BPS's own KAPITA returns 8.2524 / 6.5996 / 10.7176 and Gini 0.36285 / 0.38318 / 0.29525 — the published figures exactly. This is asserted inside the code, so if the poverty lines or the domain logic were wrong, the run would stop. Everything below is a departure from a verified baseline.

Urban and rural

The transfer reduces urban poverty more: 0.381 pp (se 0.066) against 0.244 pp (se 0.051) in rural areas, both strongly significant. That follows directly from section 8 — if three-quarters of recipients are urban, the poverty effect lands there, even though rural poverty is far higher (10.72% vs 6.60%). The programme's geography works against the place where poverty is concentrated.

10 Inequality and cost-effectiveness

In one line: MBG moves poverty but not inequality, and costs about Rp 2 juta per month per person kept out of poverty.

The Gini effect is 0.0016 — essentially nothing. That is expected: the transfer is worth 3.7% of a recipient household's spending, and recipients are spread fairly evenly across the distribution. A programme has to be both large and well-targeted to move an inequality measure.

Cost-effectiveness at ρ = 0. Monthly transfer value divided by people kept out of poverty.
ValuationTransfer per monthPeople liftedRp per person
S1 nationalRp 1,830 bn923,2571,981,659
S2 regionalRp 1,805 bn885,4122,038,217
S3 programme costRp 2,387 bn1,290,8741,849,191

Read this as an accounting ratio, not an efficiency verdict — MBG is a nutrition and schooling programme whose poverty effect is a by-product, so comparing this figure to a pure cash transfer would be unfair to it.

11 What we're confident about, and what we're not

In one line: the valuation and the poverty numbers are solid; the crowd-out assumption and the single-week snapshot are the soft spots.
ClaimHow solidWhy
The baseline matches BPS exactlyCertainAsserted in code; reproduces all 116 domains
Rp 7,491 per mealStrongPlacebo distribution passes; robust to controls (1.4%) and to the selection rule
≈923,000 people kept out of povertyStrongDesign-based CI [0.239, 0.413] pp; holds across valuations
Urban impact > rural impactStrongNon-overlapping pattern, and consistent with the allocation data
Crowd-out is near zeroWeakPoint estimate says yes, confidence interval says nothing
Regional differences in meal valueModerateStatistically real, but interpretation (tray composition) is inference
This describes the programme generallyNoOne week, mid-rollout, 14% household coverage

Things to keep remembering

  • The transfer is already in the official numbers. This is not "MBG's effect on poverty" in a behavioural sense — it is how much of the measured 8.25% is attributable to the programme being counted.
  • The value cap matters. We never remove more than a household's recorded in-kind food. Without that cap the impact reads 0.351 pp instead of 0.326 — a 7% overstatement.
  • Poverty lines are held fixed at the published provincial urban/rural values, and each household is judged against its own line whatever domain it appears in. That is BPS practice and it is why the baseline reproduces exactly.
  • Kabupaten is identifiable (514 codes, coverage ranging 0–50.6%), which we only discovered late. It opens the door to area-level designs if a pre-period round is obtained.

If picking this up again

  • Everything runs on the original BPS files. The replicated blok43 file is validation evidence and must never be merged into an analysis file.
  • Two Stata traps cost time: tempfiles created inside a program vanish when it exits, and export delimited writes value labels, so a later import reads strings not numbers.
  • Not yet done: the paper outline, Romano–Wolf robustness (rwolf not installed), and a bootstrap interval for the Gini change.
